title: Challenge to police hearings denied
article: The British Columbia Court of Appeal has ruled that complainants should have a limited role in public hearings into alleged police misconduct.
The Court of Appeal found that "a complainant has no right to participate during the evidentiary phase of a hearing" called by the Office of the Police Complaint Commissioner.

In a unanimous 3-0 ruling, written by Chief Justice Lance Finch, the court said the legislature intended to limit the involvement of complainants to making submissions at the end of any hearing, according to the provisions of the Police Act.
The court dismissed an appeal by Julie Berg, the sister of Jeffrey Michael Berg, who died after a confrontation with a Vancouver police officer in October, 2000.
Mr. Berg, 37, was a home-invasion suspect, and an autopsy concluded he died as a result of an aneurysm caused by a blow to the neck.

Vancouver police conducted an internal investigation, and more than two years after the death of Mr. Berg, the Ministry of the Attorney-General decided criminal charges against the officer were not warranted.

The Office of the Police Complaint Commissioner ordered a public hearing because of what it described as the "flawed nature" of the Vancouver police investigation. (The agency has jurisdiction to hear complaints against the 11 municipalities in B.C. that have their own local police force.)

Constable David Bruce-Thomas testified at the 2004 hearing that he kicked Mr. Berg once in the groin area and also "karate kicked" him in the midsection. Two independent witnesses testified that the officer hit Mr. Berg with his gun and kicked him several times on the ground while he was handcuffed.

Retired provincial court judge Brian Weddell was appointed as the adjudicator of the hearing. He concluded the officer did not use excessive force. The Police Complaint Commissioner declined a request by Ms. Berg to file an appeal of this ruling.
The lawyer representing Ms. Berg was denied the right to "full standing" at the hearing and was not able to cross-examine witnesses.

A spokesman for police complaint commissioner Dirk Ryneveld said yesterday that the agency was in meetings and could not comment on the Court of Appeal ruling. The spokesman added that Mr. Ryneveld's views on this issue are included in a 2005 White Paper, posted on its website.

In the white paper, Mr. Ryneveld states he does not believe the "automatic participation" of complainants will improve public hearings. He adds that the hearings are disciplinary proceedings where "the respondent \[officer\] is the person in greatest jeopardy."

"The worst-case scenario for the officer is that he would lose his job," said Ms. Berg, questioning Mr. Ryneveld's interpretation of who is most affected by a hearing into alleged police misconduct. "For my brother, the worst case has already happened."
Ms. Berg suggested the current police complaint process contains an "illusion of accountability" and the only way to try to get direct answers is to file a civil suit.
She has not filed one, though, in part because of the expense. "You are up against police unions and their lawyers, all paid out of public funds."

In his 1994 report on policing in B.C., Mr. Justice Wally Oppal concluded there was a "compelling need for strong independent civilian oversight" of police. Ms. Berg said now that Mr. Oppal is the provincial Attorney-General, she hopes he will act on his recommendations of 12 years ago.
